hints: Look at what changes from D to E, a Br atom is lost along with H from a neighbouring carbon to form a C=C double bond, so decide if this is substitution or elimination.
walkthrough:
Spot the type of change**
You start with $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and you end with $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$. No Br remains and a double bond appears. That means $\text{HBr}$ has been removed from adjacent carbons, so this is an elimination reaction, not substitution to an alcohol.

Choose the correct condition for elimination**
Remember the classic pair: aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ gives substitution to an alcohol, while $\text{NaOH}$ dissolved in ethanol with heat favours elimination to an alkene. So you need ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$ and heat.
Final answer: Ethanolic / alcoholic $\text{NaOH}$, heated under reflux.

hints: Recall that addition polymerisation opens the C=C double bond to give single bonds only, with each alkene carbon gaining one new bond to the next unit.
walkthrough:
Open the double bond**
Take E, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$. In addition polymerisation the $\pi$ bond breaks and each C of the double bond forms a new $\sigma$ bond to the next monomer. So $\text{CH=CH}$ becomes $\text{CH-CH}$ in the chain.

Draw one linked unit**
Draw $-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-$ with two long continuation bonds at each end. Each backbone carbon keeps its $\text{H}$ and its $\text{CH}_3$ group. This is poly(but-2-ene).
Final answer: Repeat unit: $-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{3})-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_{3})-$ with continuation bonds through the chain, showing trans arrangement of $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups.

hints: Identify F as butan-2-ol and E as but-2-ene, then think about what small molecule must be lost when an alcohol becomes an alkene.
walkthrough:
Write the two structures as formulas**
F is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ with formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$. E is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$ with formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$.

Balance by adding water**
Going from alcohol to alkene you lose the $\text{OH}$ plus an $\text{H}$ from the next carbon, which is $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. So the balanced equation is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_8 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3} \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{CH=CHCH}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

hints: Think about what happens when the C-Br bond in D breaks in aqueous ethanol to release bromide ions, and what silver ions do with halide ions.
walkthrough:
Follow the bromide ions**
In reaction 2, D hydrolyses slowly to release $\text{Br}^-$ ions into solution. $\text{Ag}^+$ from $\text{AgNO}_3$ then combines with $\text{Br}^-$ to give insoluble silver bromide.

Recall the colour**
Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream to off-white, silver iodide is yellow. Since D is a bromoalkane, expect a cream precipitate.
Final answer: Cream / off-white precipitate of $\text{AgBr}$ forms.

hints: Recognise that F is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, which contains the $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)}$ group that gives a positive iodoform test.
Think about how the $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)}$ fragment is split, one part becomes the yellow solid and the rest of the carbon chain becomes a carboxylate ion in alkali.
walkthrough:
Confirm the positive group**
F is butan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Any alcohol with $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}$ gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline $\text{I}_2$. That yellow solid is always $\text{CHI}_3$, triiodomethane.

Work out the leftover fragment**
The $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}$ part is cut off to make $\text{CHI}_3$. The remaining $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$ part attached to the original $\text{CH}$ carbon is oxidised to a carboxylate in alkali. That gives propanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2^-$.
Final answer: yellow precipitate: $\text{CHI}_{3}$ / triiodomethane / iodoform\norganic ion: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}^{-}$ / propanoate

hints: Compare D and G, the Br atom is directly replaced by a CN group with no change in carbon skeleton or double bond formation.
walkthrough:
Compare atoms in and out**
D has $\text{Br}$ on carbon 2, G has $\text{CN}$ on the same carbon. The carbon chain is unchanged. One group has simply swapped for another.

Name the type**
Replacement of $\text{Br}$ by $\text{CN}^-$ acting as a nucleophile is nucleophilic substitution. Accept substitution for this paper.
Final answer: substitution / nucleophilic substitution

hints: Look at the change from $\text{CN}$ in G to $\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$ in H and recall what happens to carboxylic acids with $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$.
walkthrough:
See hydrogen being added**
G contains $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$. H contains $\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. Lots of hydrogen atoms have been added across the triple bond, which is reduction.

Link to the given clue**
You are told $\text{LiAlH}_4$ reduces carboxylic acids to alcohols by donating hydride. Here it does the same job, donating hydrogen to reduce the nitrile to a primary amine, so it acts as a reducing agent.
Final answer: reducing agent / reductant

hints: Scan the spectrum for a sharp absorption in the middle region around 2200 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ where very few other bonds absorb.
Use Table 4.1 to match that wavenumber to a bond, then check which of D, E, F, G or H contains that bond.
walkthrough:
Pick out the unique peak**
Look along the spectrum. There is a clear sharp dip at about 2200 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. Table 4.1 shows $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ in nitriles absorbs at 2200 to 2250 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. No other listed group absorbs there.

Match to the compound**
Only G, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(CN)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, contains a $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ group. D contains C-Br, E contains C=C, F contains O-H, H contains N-H, none of which fit this peak. So the spectrum must be G.
Final answer: G\nAbsorption at 2200-2250 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ / nitrile, only G contains this group.

hints: Recall that bromine has two isotopes, $^{79}\text{Br}$ and $^{81}\text{Br}$, in almost equal natural abundance, so a molecule with one Br shows two molecular ion peaks two mass units apart.
walkthrough:
Think about the isotopes present**
D contains one Br atom. Bromine exists as $^{79}\text{Br}$ and $^{81}\text{Br}$ in roughly equal amounts. So some molecules of D have mass M and some have mass M+2.

Predict the height**
Because the two isotopes are about 50:50, the M peak and the M+2 peak will have almost the same intensity. If M is 3.4, M+2 is also about 3.4.
Final answer: 3.4, because $^{79}\text{Br}$:$^{81}\text{Br}$ is about 50:50 / 1:1 so M and M+2 peaks have equal abundance.
